claim: Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (ACM Computing Surveys survey): serializable concurrency control assumes short transactions, while design and software environments have operations of minutes to hours, nondeterministic user steps and people who need to see each other's work.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey) sort the answers for long units into three groups: keep serializability but cope with length; relax it using semantics (sagas, conflict predicates, split/join); coordinate people (check-out/check-in, private databases, copy/modify/merge, notification, cooperating transaction groups).

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey) measure no gain for the long-transaction mechanisms: they say the lack of performance metrics to evaluate them is unsolved, that they had found only one empirical study (Yeh and others 1987), and that many of these have not been implemented in any system.
Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): long transactions range from hours to weeks, and some last several minutes or hours, such as compiling code.
handles: long transaction duration hours to weeks

claim: Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): long transactions make automatic aborts more likely, to avoid deadlock or after failing optimistic validation.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): a user who has invested many hours in a transaction and finds at commit that it violated a consistency constraint would oppose deleting all the work by rollback, and might reverse only some of the operations explicitly.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey), citing Pradel and others 1986: snapshot validation counts only conflicts on data read before the other transaction ended as serious; a starving long transaction gets a substitute transaction with the same read and write sets that validates first; the survey calls locking the whole database for the starver unacceptable, and says the longer a transaction the greater the starvation risk.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): on failure or automatic abort, user-supplied compensation functions run for each committed transaction instead of a rollback; the bug-fix example (edit a file, compile source code, run the debugger) is modelled as a saga.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey), check-out/check-in: a long transaction works in a private database; a short transaction on the public database sets a permanent lock if nobody holds the object conflictingly and copies the object to the private database; if it is held, the user is told and the short transaction aborts.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey), Sun NSE optimistic copy/modify/merge: on conflict the users merge their changes instead of rolling back, each finisher merging with the version already deposited; a resync command tells a developer which objects others changed since the copy was taken.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey), Gordion notification: a conflict is notified to the writers as soon as it occurs or only when one attempts to commit, and a person resolves it; the survey warns that humans might not really resolve conflicts, resulting in inconsistent data.
Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey), Infuse: modules of an experimental database need only be self-consistent before they are deposited upward in the hierarchy.

Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987 (Sagas, SIGMOD pp. 249-259): a long-lived transaction is a sequence of sub-transactions that can interleave with other transactions; each has a compensating transaction, and on failure the committed ones are compensated in reverse order.

Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987 (Sagas): the paper names two recovery forms, backward recovery (compensate) and forward recovery (resume from a save-point), and logs saga state so that a running saga can be finished or compensated after a failure.

Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987 (Sagas): a saga's compensation is semantic and cannot simply store and restore an earlier value, because other transactions may run in between (seat-count example); a saga may view the partial results of other sagas.

Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987 (Sagas) report no measured gain: the abstract says the idea has the potential to improve performance significantly, but the text has no simulation, experiment, measurement or figure (word search found none).

Bancilhon, Kim and Korth 1985 (VLDB, A Model of CAD Transactions): conventional transactions terminate within a few seconds, so preventing access and backing out all updates on failure is reasonable there; CAD transactions are long and involve conscious decisions of human designers.

Bancilhon, Kim and Korth 1985: a designer's transaction is a set of short transactions in a six-level hierarchy; a system abort (deadlock or crash) aborts only the current short transaction, not the enclosing cooperating transaction, and an explicit abort of a higher level aborts everything beneath it.
Bancilhon, Kim and Korth 1985 report no measured gain: the paper is a formal model with no implementation or figure.

Bancilhon, Kim and Korth 1985 assume that a person decides the consistency predicate and recovery procedure at each level, and that projects partition the data so that a cross-project wait is acceptable.

Pu, Kaiser and Hutchinson 1988 (split-transactions, VLDB pp. 26-37): a long transaction loses its finished work to rollback at abort, and keeps its updated resources locked for its whole duration, which makes them a concurrency bottleneck.

Pu, Kaiser and Hutchinson 1988: Split-Transaction divides an ongoing transaction into two serializable transactions, one of which commits its part and releases it while the other continues; Join-Transaction merges a finished one into a target; both are allowed only when the read and write sets let the two serialize.
Pu, Kaiser and Hutchinson 1988 report no experiment: the paper is a design with algorithms, applied by example in section 3 (a programming environment, a CAD tool, a type-specification split).

Pu, Kaiser and Hutchinson 1988 assume that the transaction is quiescent when it is split, that the programmer or tool can name the read and write sets of both halves, and that the database keeps versions.
Perry, Siy and Votta 2001 (TOSEM 10(3):308-337) study one of 50 subsystems of the 5ESS switch over 12 years, April 1984 to April 1996, with a peak of 200 developers and 50 at the end.
Perry, Siy and Votta 2001, in the 5ESS subsystem studied (observational): 12.5% of all deltas are made to the same file by different developers within 24 hours of each other.

Perry, Siy and Votta 2001, in the 5ESS subsystem studied (observational): 3% of the deltas made within 24 hours by different developers physically overlap each other's changes; the authors believe semantic interference causes many more conflicts, which they did not measure.

Perry, Siy and Votta 2001, in the 5ESS subsystem studied (observational): 55% of files never had more than one modification request open at a time, about 30% had up to 2 parallel requests per day, and 0.6% had more than 6.

Perry, Siy and Votta 2001, in the 5ESS subsystem studied (observational): files with a high degree of parallel development correlate significantly with defect counts, also after accounting for lifetime, size and number of deltas; correlation 0.63 for PCdays with defect count and 0.62 for the weighted count; a correlation, not a controlled effect.

Perry, Siy and Votta 2001, citing Leblang 1994 (read only as cited there): ClearCase automatically merged over 90% of changed files, and in about 1% of cases the merge tool made an inappropriate automatic decision.
Perry, Siy and Votta 2001: it is not clear how well current merge technologies will support this degree of parallel versions when changes interfere.
Perry, Siy and Votta 2001, in the 5ESS subsystem studied: 46% of IMRs and 50% of MRs are opened and solved on the same day, so the other half last longer.
